title: relate the average rate of change over an interval to the instantaneous rate for a quadratic position function, solving
stem: A particle moves along a line so that its position is s(t) = t² − 5t + 3 meters at time t seconds. At what time t, with 1 < t < 7, is the instantaneous velocity equal to the average velocity over the interval [1, 7]?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The number 3 is the value of the average velocity in meters per second, not a time. The time comes from solving s′(t) = 3.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Solving s′(t) = 2t − 5 = 0 finds when the particle is momentarily at rest, which is a different question from matching the average velocity.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This solves 2t − 5 = 18, using the total change s(7) − s(1) = 18 without dividing by the interval length 6. The result also lies outside the interval (1, 7).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: The average velocity is (s(7) − s(1))/6 = (17 − (−1))/6 = 3. Setting s′(t) = 2t − 5 = 3 gives t = 4, which lies in (1, 7).

choices.label: D

title: decide what a net change over an interval does and does not tell you: average rate, not instantaneous rate or constant r
stem: The amount of water in a tank is W(t) gallons, where t is measured in hours. It is known that W(2) = 90 and W(8) = 60. Which statement must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The net change in the water from t = 2 to t = 8 is −30 gallons, so the average rate of change over that interval is −5 gallons per hour.
choices.rationale: Correct: The net change is W(8) − W(2) = −30 gallons over 6 hours, so the average rate is −30/6 = −5 gallons per hour. Only this average is guaranteed by two data points.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The average rate over [2, 8] need not equal the instantaneous rate at the midpoint. W′(5) could be any value, since only the two endpoint values are known.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tank lost exactly 5 gallons during every hour from t = 2 to t = 8.
choices.rationale: An average of −5 gallons per hour is compatible with a leak that speeds up and slows down. The data do not show a constant rate in each hour.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average rate of change of the water from t = 2 to t = 8 is −30 gallons per hour.
choices.rationale: The net change −30 is the change in gallons, not a rate. It must be divided by the interval length 6 hours to get the average rate in gallons per hour.

title: decide what a net change over an interval does and does not tell you: average rate, not instantaneous rate or constant r (variant 1)
stem: The temperature of an oven is T(t) degrees Celsius after t minutes. It is known that T(10) = 180 and T(25) = 255. Which statement must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The temperature rose by a net 75 degrees Celsius from t = 10 to t = 25, an average of 5 degrees Celsius per minute.
choices.rationale: Correct: The net change is T(25) − T(10) = 75 degrees over 15 minutes, so the average rate of change is 75/15 = 5 degrees Celsius per minute.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The midpoint of [10, 25] is 17.5, but an average rate over an interval does not force the instantaneous rate at the midpoint to equal it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The oven was heating at 5 degrees Celsius per minute at the moment t = 25.
choices.rationale: The average over [10, 25] says nothing specific about the rate at the endpoint t = 25, where the oven could be heating faster or slower.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average rate of change of temperature on [10, 25] is 75 degrees Celsius per minute.
choices.rationale: The change of 75 degrees must be divided by the 15-minute length of the interval. As a rate, 75 degrees per minute is far too large.

title: decide what a net change over an interval does and does not tell you: average rate, not instantaneous rate or constant r (variant 2)

title: decide what a net change over an interval does and does not tell you: average rate, not instantaneous rate or constant r (variant 3)
stem: The depth of a river is D(x) meters at a point x meters from the bank. It is known that D(2) = 3.5 and D(10) = 1.5. Which statement must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The depth decreases by exactly 0.25 meter for each meter moved from x = 2 to x = 10.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average rate of change of depth on [2, 10] is −2 meters per meter.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: The depth decreases by a net 2 meters from x = 2 to x = 10, an average of 0.25 meter of depth per meter of distance.
choices.rationale: Correct: The net change is D(10) − D(2) = −2 meters over 8 meters of distance, an average rate of −2/8 = −0.25 meter per meter (a decrease of 0.25).

title: identify the function and point behind a difference-quotient limit and evaluate it as a derivative.
stem: The limit lim(x→3) (x⁴ − 81)/(x − 3) equals f′(a) for some function f and number a. What is the value of the limit?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: With f(x) = x⁴ and a = 3, the limit is f′(3) = 4 · 3³ = 108.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The number 81 is f(3) for f(x) = x⁴, not the derivative. The limit is the slope f′(3), not the function value.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This differentiates x⁴ as 4x⁴, keeping the exponent 4 instead of lowering it to 3. The correct power rule gives 4x³.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This computes 4 · 3 instead of 4 · 3³. It lowers the exponent in the original function but then forgets to apply it to the evaluated point.

title: identify the function and point behind a difference-quotient limit and evaluate it as a derivative. (variant 1)

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

title: identify the function and point behind a difference-quotient limit and evaluate it as a derivative. (variant 2)
stem: The limit lim(h→0) [(1 + h)⁻² − 1]/h equals f′(a) for some function f and number a. What is the value of the limit?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This drops the negative sign. Differentiating x⁻² gives −2x⁻³, which is negative at x = 1.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The number 1 is f(1) = 1⁻², the function value rather than the derivative at x = 1.

title: identify the function and point behind a difference-quotient limit and evaluate it as a derivative. (variant 3)
stem: The limit lim(x→−2) (x³ + 8)/(x + 2) equals f′(a) for some function f and number a. What is the value of the limit?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The number −8 is f(−2) = (−2)³, not the derivative. The limit is the slope of f at −2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses 3x instead of 3x², so it does not square −2. The power rule gives f′(x) = 3x², which is positive.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The numerator and denominator both approach 0, but that does not make the limit 0. It is f′(−2) for f(x) = x³.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: With f(x) = x³ and a = −2, the limit is f′(−2) = 3(−2)² = 12.

title: find the error in a limit-definition derivation where f(x + h) is expanded incorrectly, and state the correct derivative
stem: A student uses the definition to find f′(x) for f(x) = x². The student writes f(x + h) = x² + h², so [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h = h²/h = h, and concludes f′(x) = lim(h→0) h = 0. Which statement identifies the error and gives the correct derivative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h², so the correct derivative is 2x + h.
choices.rationale: This finds the right expansion but stops before taking the limit. The difference quotient is 2x + h, and the derivative is its limit as h → 0, which is 2x.

choices.label: B
choices.text: (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h², not x² + h², so the correct derivative is f′(x) = 2x.
choices.rationale: Correct: The correct expansion gives [x² + 2xh + h² − x²]/h = 2x + h, whose limit as h → 0 is 2x.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is no error. The terms in h vanish as h → 0, so the derivative of x² is 0 for every x.
choices.rationale: The squared binomial has a middle term 2xh that the student dropped. A derivative of 0 would make x² constant, which it is not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h², so the correct derivative is 2.
choices.rationale: This divides 2xh by xh instead of by h, losing a factor of x. The difference quotient is 2x + h, which tends to 2x.

title: find the error in a limit-definition derivation where f(x + h) is expanded incorrectly, and state the correct derivative (variant 1)
stem: A student uses the definition to find f′(x) for f(x) = x³. The student writes f(x + h) = x³ + h³, so [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h = h³/h = h², and concludes f′(x) = lim(h→0) h² = 0. Which statement identifies the error and gives the correct derivative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: (x + h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³, so the correct derivative is 3x² + 3xh + h².
choices.rationale: This stops before taking the limit. The difference quotient is 3x² + 3xh + h², and the derivative is its limit as h → 0, which is 3x².

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is no error. Both h² and h vanish as h → 0, so the derivative of x³ is 0.
choices.rationale: The cube expansion has two cross terms the student dropped. A derivative of 0 would make x³ constant, which it is not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: (x + h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³, not x³ + h³, so the correct derivative is f′(x) = 3x².
choices.rationale: Correct: The correct expansion gives [3x²h + 3xh² + h³]/h = 3x² + 3xh + h², whose limit as h → 0 is 3x².

choices.label: D
choices.text: (x + h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³, so the correct derivative is 3x.
choices.rationale: This lowers the exponent but loses a factor of x. The terms 3x²h and 3xh² give a difference quotient that tends to 3x², not 3x.

title: find the error in a limit-definition derivation where f(x + h) is expanded incorrectly, and state the correct derivative (variant 2)
stem: A student uses the definition to find f′(x) for f(x) = 1/x. The student writes 1/(x + h) = 1/x + 1/h, so the numerator is 1/h and the quotient is 1/h², and concludes the derivative does not exist. Which statement identifies the error and gives the correct derivative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1/(x + h) is not 1/x + 1/h; using a common denominator gives f′(x) = 1/x².
choices.rationale: This finds the right fix but loses the sign. The numerator x − (x + h) equals −h, so the limit is negative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1/(x + h) is not 1/x + 1/h; using a common denominator gives f′(x) = −1/x².
choices.rationale: Correct: [1/(x + h) − 1/x]/h = [x − (x + h)]/[x(x + h)h] = −1/[x(x + h)], whose limit as h → 0 is −1/x².

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is no error. The quotient 1/h² is unbounded as h → 0, so 1/x has no derivative.
choices.rationale: A reciprocal of a sum is not the sum of reciprocals. The function 1/x is differentiable for x ≠ 0, so the conclusion is wrong.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1/(x + h) is not 1/x + 1/h; using a common denominator gives f′(x) = −1/x.
choices.rationale: This keeps the sign but misses the factor 1/x² in the common denominator. The limit of −1/(x(x + h)) is −1/x², not −1/x.

title: find the error in a limit-definition derivation where f(x + h) is expanded incorrectly, and state the correct derivative (variant 3)
stem: A student uses the definition to find f′(x) for f(x) = √x with x > 0. The student writes √(x + h) = √x + √h, so the quotient is √h/h = 1/√h, and concludes the derivative does not exist. Which statement identifies the error and gives the correct derivative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: √(x + h) is not √x + √h; multiplying by the conjugate gives f′(x) = 1/√x.
choices.rationale: This multiplies by the conjugate correctly but drops the 2. The denominator √(x + h) + √x tends to 2√x, not √x.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is no error. The quotient 1/√h is unbounded as h → 0, so √x has no derivative for x > 0.
choices.rationale: A square root of a sum is not the sum of square roots. The function √x is differentiable for every x > 0.

choices.label: C
choices.text: √(x + h) is not √x + √h; multiplying by the conjugate gives f′(x) = 1/(2√x).
choices.rationale: Correct: [√(x + h) − √x]/h = 1/[√(x + h) + √x], whose limit as h → 0 is 1/(2√x).

choices.label: D
choices.text: √(x + h) is not √x + √h; multiplying by the conjugate gives f′(x) = 1/(2x).
choices.rationale: This keeps the factor 2 but replaces √x with x in the denominator. The conjugate denominator tends to 2√x.

title: estimate acceleration from a table of velocity values with uneven spacing, then use the signs of velocity and accelerati
stem:
The velocity v(t), in meters per second, of a car moving along a straight road is given in the table for selected times t in seconds.
t (seconds):   0   3   7   12
v(t) (m/s):   −4   −10   −16   −22
Using the table values closest to t = 5, which statement is best at t = 5?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The acceleration is about −1.5 m/s² and the car is slowing down.
choices.rationale: Velocity and acceleration have the same sign (both negative), so the speed is increasing. A negative acceleration slows an object down only when the velocity is positive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The acceleration is about −1.5 m/s² and the car is speeding up.
choices.rationale: Correct: a(5) ≈ (v(7) − v(3))/(7 − 3) = (−16 − (−10))/4 = −1.5 m/s². Since v < 0 and a < 0, the speed is increasing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The acceleration is about −6 m/s² and the car is speeding up.
choices.rationale: The change in velocity over [3, 7] is −6, but it must be divided by the interval length 4 to estimate acceleration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The acceleration is about 1.5 m/s² and the car is slowing down.
choices.rationale: This subtracts the values in the wrong order, giving +1.5 instead of −1.5. The velocity is becoming more negative, so the acceleration estimate is negative.

title: use the monotonic behaviour of f′ to bracket f′(a) between the slopes of secant lines on either side of a.
stem:
The table gives selected values of a differentiable function f. It is also known that f′ is increasing on the interval [2, 10].
x:   2   5   10
f(x):   7   13   31
Which statement about f′(5) must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The average of the two secant slopes is 2.8, but with only three data points nothing forces f′(5) to equal it.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: The secant slope on [2, 5] is (13 − 7)/3 = 2 and on [5, 10] is (31 − 13)/5 = 3.6. With f′ increasing, f′(5) lies strictly between them.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The slope of the secant over [5, 10] is 3.6. Since f′ is increasing, f′(5) is below the average of f′ on [5, 10], so f′(5) < 3.6.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The slope of the secant over [2, 5] is 2. Since f′ is increasing, f′(5) is above the average of f′ on [2, 5], so f′(5) > 2.

title: use the monotonic behaviour of f′ to bracket f′(a) between the slopes of secant lines on either side of a. (variant 1)

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The slope of the secant over [4, 9] is 3. Since f′ is decreasing, f′(4) is above the average of f′ on [4, 9], so f′(4) > 3.

title: use the monotonic behaviour of f′ to bracket f′(a) between the slopes of secant lines on either side of a. (variant 2)
stem:
The table gives selected values of a differentiable function g. It is also known that g′ is increasing on the interval [0, 4].
x:   0   3   4
g(x):   2   8   12
Which statement about g′(3) must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The slope of the secant over [0, 4] is 2.5, but the endpoint-to-endpoint slope is not guaranteed to equal g′(3) at an interior point.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The slope of the secant over [3, 4] is 4. Since g′ is increasing, g′(3) is below the average of g′ on [3, 4], so g′(3) < 4.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The slope of the secant over [0, 3] is 2. Since g′ is increasing, g′(3) is above the average of g′ on [0, 3], so g′(3) > 2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: The secant slopes are (8 − 2)/3 = 2 on [0, 3] and (12 − 8)/1 = 4 on [3, 4]. With g′ increasing, g′(3) lies between 2 and 4.

title: use the monotonic behaviour of f′ to bracket f′(a) between the slopes of secant lines on either side of a. (variant 3)
stem:
The table gives the population P(t), in thousands, of a town at selected times t in years. It is also known that P′ is decreasing on the interval [2, 8].
t:   2   6   8
P(t):   50   90   100
Which statement about P′(6) must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The average of the two secant slopes is 7.5, but the data do not force P′(6) to equal it.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: The secant slopes are (90 − 50)/4 = 10 on [2, 6] and (100 − 90)/2 = 5 on [6, 8]. With P′ decreasing, P′(6) lies between 5 and 10.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The slope of the secant over [2, 6] is 10 thousand per year. Since P′ is decreasing, P′(6) is below the average of P′ on [2, 6], so P′(6) < 10.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The slope of the secant over [6, 8] is 5 thousand per year. Since P′ is decreasing, P′(6) is above the average of P′ on [6, 8], so P′(6) > 5.

title: choose constants that make a piecewise function both continuous and differentiable at the join, using the slopes and val
stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = x³ for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = ax + b for x > 1. For which values of a and b is f differentiable at x = 1?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Continuity needs a(1) + b = 1³ = 1. Equal slopes need a = 3x² at x = 1, so a = 3, and then b = 1 − 3 = −2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Matching the slope gives a = 3, but b = 1 leaves the pieces disconnected: 3 + 1 = 4 does not equal f(1) = 1, so f is not even continuous.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Continuity alone holds with a + b = 1, but the slopes are 3 and 1, so the graph has a corner at x = 1 and f is not differentiable there.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This sets a = 3 correctly but solves a − b = 1 instead of a + b = 1. At x = 1 the right piece is 3 + 2 = 5, not 1.

title: choose constants that make a piecewise function both continuous and differentiable at the join, using the slopes and val (variant 1)
stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = ax² + b for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = x³ − 2x for x > 2. For which values of a and b is f differentiable at x = 2?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Continuity needs 4a + b = 2³ − 2(2) = 4. Equal slopes need 2a(2) = 3(2²) − 2 = 10, so a = 5/2, and then b = 4 − 10 = −6.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Continuity needs 4a + b = 4, which a = 1, b = 0 satisfies, but the slopes are 4 and 10, so f has a corner at x = 2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This matches the slopes with a = 5/2 but sets b equal to the right-hand value 4, forgetting that b = 4 − 4a. Then 4a + b = 14, so f jumps.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This matches the slopes but solves 4a + b = −4 instead of 4. The pieces then disagree at x = 2, so f is not continuous.

title: choose constants that make a piecewise function both continuous and differentiable at the join, using the slopes and val (variant 2)
stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = ax + b for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = 1/x for x > 2. For which values of a and b is f differentiable at x = 2?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The slope matches with a = −1/4, but b = 1/2 is the value of 1/x at 2 and ignores that the left piece must equal 1/2 at x = 2, which requires 2a + b = 1/2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Continuity needs 2a + b = 1/2. Equal slopes need a = −1/x² at x = 2, so a = −1/4, and then b = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses the slope of 1/x with the wrong sign. The derivative of 1/x is −1/x², which is −1/4 at x = 2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: With a = −1/4 and b = 0 the left piece equals −1/2 at x = 2, not 1/2, so f is not continuous.

title: choose constants that make a piecewise function both continuous and differentiable at the join, using the slopes and val (variant 3)
stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = ax² + bx for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 2 ln x + 3 for x > 1. For which values of a and b is f differentiable at x = 1?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This satisfies continuity (1 + 2 = 3), but the left slope is 2a + b = 4 while the right slope is 2, so the graph has a corner at x = 1.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The slope condition 2a + b = 2 holds, but a + b = 1 while the right piece equals 3 at x = 1, so f has a jump at x = 1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This ignores the +3 in the right piece, matching a + b to 2 ln 1 = 0. The right piece actually equals 3 at x = 1, so f has a jump there.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: Continuity needs a + b = 2 ln 1 + 3 = 3. Equal slopes need 2a + b = 2/x = 2 at x = 1. Subtracting gives a = −1, so b = 4.

title: count the points where the absolute value of a polynomial fails to be differentiable by telling simple roots from repeat
stem: Let f(x) = |(x − 2)²(x + 1)|. At how many values of x is f not differentiable?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Near x = 2, (x − 2)²(x + 1) is positive, so f equals the smooth polynomial there. Only the sign change at x = −1 produces a corner, so there is 1 point.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The absolute value of a polynomial can have corners where the polynomial crosses zero. At x = −1 the factor x + 1 changes sign, so there is a corner there.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Counting both zeros forgets that (x − 2)² does not change sign at x = 2. Near 2, f(x) = (x − 2)²(x + 1), which is smooth.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Counting the roots with multiplicity (2 at x = 2 and 1 at x = −1) does not reflect where the graph has corners. Only a sign change creates one.

title: count the points where the absolute value of a polynomial fails to be differentiable by telling simple roots from repeat (variant 1)
stem: Let f(x) = |x(x − 3)²(x + 2)|. At how many values of x is f not differentiable?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Counting all three zeros ignores that (x − 3)² does not change sign at x = 3, so f is smooth there.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Counting only one zero misses that both x and x + 2 change sign. Each simple root gives a corner in the absolute value.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The absolute value is not automatically differentiable where the inside is. At a simple root such as x = 0 the one-sided slopes are opposite.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: The factors x and x + 2 each change sign once, giving corners at x = 0 and x = −2. The squared factor leaves f smooth at x = 3, so there are 2 points.

title: count the points where the absolute value of a polynomial fails to be differentiable by telling simple roots from repeat (variant 2)
stem: Let f(x) = |(x − 1)³(x + 2)²|. At how many values of x is f not differentiable?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The triple root is a trap: (x − 1)³ changes sign, but |(x − 1)³| = |x − 1|³ has one-sided slopes that both equal 0 at x = 1, so there is no corner.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Counting both distinct zeros assumes every zero produces a corner. A zero of order 2 or higher, with a vanishing derivative, does not.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Adding the multiplicities (3 + 2) counts something unrelated to corners of the graph.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: At x = 1, f(x) = |x − 1|³(x + 2)², whose derivative from both sides is 0. At x = −2 the squared factor does not change sign. So f is differentiable everywhere.

title: count the points where the absolute value of a polynomial fails to be differentiable by telling simple roots from repeat (variant 3)
stem: Let f(x) = |x³ − 9x|. At how many values of x is f not differentiable?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: x³ − 9x = x(x − 3)(x + 3) has three simple roots at 0, 3 and −3. Each is a sign change with nonzero slope, so the absolute value has three corners.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The zeros are x = 0, 3 and −3. Counting only x = 0 ignores that the polynomial also crosses zero at x = 3 and x = −3.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Counting only the two nonzero roots forgets that the polynomial also changes sign at x = 0, where the factor x is simple.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The absolute value is not smooth where a simple root makes the inside change sign. Each of the three crossings is a corner.

title: find the points of tangency of lines drawn from an external point to a power-function curve.
stem: Two lines pass through the point (1, −3) and are tangent to the graph of y = x². What are the x-coordinates of the points of tangency?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: The tangent at x = a is y = a² + 2a(x − a). It passes through (1, −3) when −3 = a² + 2a(1 − a), so a² − 2a − 3 = 0 and a = 3 or a = −1.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The point (1, −3) is not on the parabola, since 1² = 1. It is the external point the lines pass through, not a point of tangency.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This keeps only the positive solution. The equation a² − 2a − 3 = 0 has two roots, and the second line is tangent where x = −1.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This factors a² − 2a − 3 as (a + 3)(a − 1), which expands to a² + 2a − 3. The correct factors are (a − 3)(a + 1).

title: find the points of tangency of lines drawn from an external point to a power-function curve. (variant 1)
stem: A line through the point (−2, 0) is tangent to the graph of y = √x. What is the x-coordinate of the point of tangency?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The point (−2, 0) is the external point the line passes through; it is not on the graph of √x, which is defined only for x ≥ 0.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: The tangent at x = a is y = √a + (x − a)/(2√a). It passes through (−2, 0) when 0 = √a + (−2 − a)/(2√a), so 2a = 2 + a and a = 2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The point (1, 1) is on the curve, but the tangent there is y = 1 + (x − 1)/2, which crosses the x-axis at x = −1, not at −2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: At x = 4 the tangent is y = 2 + (x − 4)/4, which crosses the x-axis at x = −4, not at −2.

title: find the points of tangency of lines drawn from an external point to a power-function curve. (variant 2)
stem: Two lines pass through the point (2, −5) and are tangent to the graph of y = x². What are the x-coordinates of the points of tangency?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This keeps only the positive root of a² − 4a − 5 = 0. The second solution a = −1 gives a second tangent line.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The x-coordinate of the given point is 2, but the point (2, −5) is not on the parabola (where y would be 4). It is the external point.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: The tangent at x = a is y = a² + 2a(x − a). It passes through (2, −5) when −5 = a² + 2a(2 − a), so a² − 4a − 5 = 0 and a = 5 or a = −1.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This factors a² − 4a − 5 as (a − 1)(a + 5), which expands to a² + 4a − 5. The correct factors are (a − 5)(a + 1).

title: find the points of tangency of lines drawn from an external point to a power-function curve. (variant 3)
stem: A line through the point (3, 0) is tangent to the graph of y = 1/x for x > 0. What is the x-coordinate of the point of tangency?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The x-coordinate of the given point is 3, but that is where the line crosses the x-axis. The point of tangency is on the curve, so its y-coordinate is not 0.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This inverts the answer. At x = 2/3 the tangent line is y = 3 − (9/4)x, which crosses the x-axis at x = 4/3, not at 3.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: The tangent at x = a is y = 2/a − x/a². It passes through (3, 0) when 2/a = 3/a², so a = 3/2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: At x = 1/3 the tangent has slope −9 and meets the x-axis at x = 2/3, not 3.

title: use the power rule to find where a rate of change numerically equals the quantity itself in a geometric context.
stem: The volume of a cube with side length s centimeters is V(s) = s³ cubic centimeters. For what positive side length is the rate of change of V with respect to s, in cubic centimeters per centimeter, numerically equal to V?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses V′(s) = 3s instead of 3s². Setting 3s = s³ gives s = √3, which is not a solution of 3s² = s³.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The value 6 comes from setting the surface area 6s² equal to the volume. The question is about the rate of change of the volume.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This inverts the result of solving 3s² = s³, which gives s = 3.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: V′(s) = 3s². Setting 3s² = s³ gives s²(3 − s) = 0, so s = 3 for s > 0.

title: use the power rule to find where a rate of change numerically equals the quantity itself in a geometric context. (variant 1)
stem: The area of a circle with radius r centimeters is A(r) = πr² square centimeters. For what positive radius is the rate of change of A with respect to r, in square centimeters per centimeter, numerically equal to A?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses A′(r) = πr instead of 2πr. Setting πr = πr² gives r = 1, which does not satisfy 2πr = πr².

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This treats r as constant when differentiating, getting A′ = 2π and then 2π = πr², so r = √2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This inverts the result of solving 2πr = πr², which gives r = 2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: A′(r) = 2πr. Setting 2πr = πr² gives r(r − 2) = 0, so r = 2 for r > 0.

title: use the power rule to find where a rate of change numerically equals the quantity itself in a geometric context. (variant 2)
stem: The amount of a drug in the bloodstream is P(x) = x^(3/2) milligrams, x hours after infusion begins. For what positive x is the rate of change of P, in milligrams per hour, numerically equal to P(x)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This squares the correct value. Setting (3/2)x^(1/2) = x^(3/2) and dividing by x^(1/2) gives x = 3/2 directly, with no further squaring.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: P′(x) = (3/2)x^(1/2). Setting (3/2)x^(1/2) = x^(3/2) and dividing by x^(1/2) gives x = 3/2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This inverts the result. The equation (3/2)x^(1/2) = x^(3/2) gives x = 3/2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses P′(x) = 3x^(1/2) by doubling the exponent instead of multiplying by 3/2. The correct coefficient is 3/2.

title: use the power rule to find where a rate of change numerically equals the quantity itself in a geometric context. (variant 3)
stem: The number of bacteria in a culture is N(t) = t⁵ thousand, t hours after the start. For what positive time t is the rate of growth, in thousands per hour, numerically equal to N(t)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This inverts the answer. The equation 5t⁴ = t⁵ gives t = 5.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the lowered exponent as the answer. The equation is 5t⁴ = t⁵, whose positive solution is the coefficient 5, not the exponent 4.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: N′(t) = 5t⁴. Setting 5t⁴ = t⁵ gives t⁴(5 − t) = 0, so t = 5 for t > 0.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This squares the correct value. Dividing 5t⁴ = t⁵ by t⁴ gives t = 5 directly.

title: use the fact that a constant term disappears under differentiation to choose the constant that makes a horizontal line t
stem: Let f(x) = x³ − 3x² + k, where k is a constant. For which values of k is the horizontal line y = 5 tangent to the graph of f?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Here f′(x) = 3x² − 6x = 0 at x = 0 and x = 2. Using only x = 0 gives f(0) = k = 5 but misses that the graph is also horizontal at x = 2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x is zero at x = 0 and x = 2. Tangency to y = 5 needs f(0) = k = 5 or f(2) = k − 4 = 5, so k = 5 or k = 9.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Using only x = 2 gives f(2) = k − 4 = 5, so k = 9, but it misses that f is also horizontal at x = 0, where f(0) = k = 5.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This has a sign error at x = 2: f(2) = 8 − 12 + k = k − 4, so f(2) = 5 gives k = 9, not k = 1.

title: use the fact that a constant term disappears under differentiation to choose the constant that makes a horizontal line t (variant 1)
stem: Let f(x) = x³ − 12x + k, where k is a constant. For which values of k is the x-axis tangent to the graph of f?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: f′(x) = 3x² − 12 is zero at x = ±2. Tangency to y = 0 needs f(2) = k − 16 = 0 or f(−2) = k + 16 = 0, so k = 16 or k = −16.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Here f′(x) = 3x² − 12 is zero at x = 2 and x = −2. The value k = 16 comes from x = 2, but x = −2 gives f(−2) = 16 + k = 0, so k = −16 also works.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The constant k does not disappear from f; it only disappears from f′. The horizontal tangent at x = ±2 needs f(±2) = 0, which fixes k.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The values ±2 are the x-coordinates where f′ = 0, not the values of k. Tangency to the x-axis needs f(±2) = 0.

title: use the fact that a constant term disappears under differentiation to choose the constant that makes a horizontal line t (variant 2)
stem: Let f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + k, where k is a constant. For which values of k is the horizontal line y = −4 tangent to the graph of f?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Here f′(x) = 6x² − 18x is zero at x = 0 and x = 3. Using only x = 0 gives f(0) = k = −4 but misses the second point of tangency at x = 3.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Using only x = 3 gives f(3) = k − 27 = −4, so k = 23, but it misses the horizontal tangent at x = 0, where f(0) = k = −4.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: f′(x) = 6x² − 18x is zero at x = 0 and x = 3. Tangency to y = −4 needs f(0) = k = −4 or f(3) = k − 27 = −4, so k = −4 or k = 23.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This reverses the sign of both values. The conditions f(0) = k = −4 and f(3) = k − 27 = −4 give k = −4 and k = 23, not 4 and −23.

title: use the fact that a constant term disappears under differentiation to choose the constant that makes a horizontal line t (variant 3)
stem: Let f(x) = x⁴ − 8x² + k, where k is a constant. For which values of k is the horizontal line y = 3 tangent to the graph of f?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Here f′(x) = 4x³ − 16x is zero at x = 0 and x = ±2. Using only x = 0 gives f(0) = k = 3 but misses the horizontal tangents at x = ±2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Using only x = ±2 gives f(±2) = k − 16 = 3, so k = 19, but it misses the horizontal tangent at x = 0, where f(0) = k = 3.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This has a sign error at x = ±2: f(±2) = 16 − 32 + k = k − 16, so f(±2) = 3 gives k = 19, not k = −13.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: f′(x) = 4x³ − 16x is zero at x = 0 and x = ±2. Tangency to y = 3 needs f(0) = k = 3 or f(±2) = k − 16 = 3, so k = 3 or k = 19.

title: work backward from a given derivative of a combination to the derivative of a component function, using the sum and cons
stem: Let f be a differentiable function, and let g(x) = 4f(x) − x². The tangent line to the graph of g at x = 2 has slope 6. What is f′(2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: g′(x) = 4f′(x) − 2x, so g′(2) = 4f′(2) − 4 = 6, which gives 4f′(2) = 10 and f′(2) = 5/2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This ignores the −x² term. From 4f′(2) = 6 it gives 3/2, but g′(x) = 4f′(x) − 2x, so at x = 2 the term −4 must be included.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This solves 4f′(2) − 4 = 6 incorrectly by subtracting 4 from 6 and not dividing by 4. The correct step is 4f′(2) = 10.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This has a sign error on the x² term: it solves 4f′(2) + 4 = 6, but the derivative of −x² is −2x, which is −4 at x = 2.

title: work backward from a given derivative of a combination to the derivative of a component function, using the sum and cons (variant 1)
stem: Let f be a differentiable function, and let g(x) = 3f(x) + x³. The tangent line to the graph of g at x = 1 has slope 12. What is f′(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This ignores the x³ term and divides 12 by 3 to get 4, but g′(x) = 3f′(x) + 3x² includes 3x² = 3 at x = 1.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This subtracts 3 from 12 but forgets to divide by the constant multiple 3. The step 3f′(1) = 9 gives f′(1) = 3.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: g′(x) = 3f′(x) + 3x², so g′(1) = 3f′(1) + 3 = 12, which gives 3f′(1) = 9 and f′(1) = 3.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This has a sign error on the x³ term: it solves 3f′(1) − 3 = 12, but the derivative of +x³ is +3x².

title: work backward from a given derivative of a combination to the derivative of a component function, using the sum and cons (variant 2)
stem: Let f be a differentiable function, and let h(x) = 5x − 2f(x). The graph of h has a horizontal tangent line at x = −1. What is f′(−1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This forgets the constant multiple 2: from 5 − 2f′(−1) = 0, f′(−1) = 5/2, not 5.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This has a sign error: it solves 5 + 2f′(−1) = 0, but the derivative of −2f(x) is −2f′(x).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This inverts the result. Solving 5 − 2f′(−1) = 0 gives f′(−1) = 5/2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: h′(x) = 5 − 2f′(x). A horizontal tangent needs h′(−1) = 5 − 2f′(−1) = 0, so f′(−1) = 5/2.

title: work backward from a given derivative of a combination to the derivative of a component function, using the sum and cons (variant 3)
stem: Let f be a differentiable function, and let p(x) = (1/2)f(x) + 6x². The tangent line to the graph of p at x = 1 has slope −5. What is f′(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This forgets to multiply by 2 to undo the constant multiple 1/2. From (1/2)f′(1) = −17, f′(1) = −34.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This differentiates 6x² as 6x instead of 12x, getting (1/2)f′(1) + 6 = −5, so f′(1) = −22.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This has a sign error: it solves (1/2)f′(1) − 12 = −5, but the derivative of +6x² is +12x, which is +12 at x = 1.

title: find where a tangent line to e^x or ln x passes through a given external point.
stem: The tangent line to the graph of y = eˣ at x = a passes through the origin. What is the value of a?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: At x = 0 the tangent line is y = 1 + x, which passes through (0, 1), not the origin. The origin's x-coordinate is not the point of tangency.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The number e is the value of eˣ at x = 1. It is the y-coordinate of the point of tangency, not the x-coordinate.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This has a sign error: the tangent y = eᵃ + eᵃ(x − a) passes through (0, 0) when 1 − a = 0, not 1 + a = 0.

title: apply the product rule to a rate in context, such as revenue as price times quantity, and interpret the result with unit
stem: A company sells q units at a price of p(q) dollars per unit, so its revenue is R(q) = q · p(q) dollars. When q = 100, the price is p(100) = 12 dollars and p′(100) = −0.05 dollar per unit. Which statement is the best interpretation of R′(100)?

stem: Let f and g be differentiable functions with f(2) = 8, g(2) = 4 and g′(2) = 3, and let h(x) = f(x)/g(x). The graph of h has a horizontal tangent line at x = 2. What is f′(2)?
